rows.en: In all these enactments the hand of Shammai was firm with him; and of the decree he made concerning the impurity of hands it is said explicitly that both of them agreed on it (Shabbat 14b). And without doubt they dealt with each other in peace and brotherhood, although they differed in their opinions. Yet one incident is told of them from which it appears that Shammai sometimes came against Hillel with his hardness of spirit and wanted to establish his opinion by force. Once a question was asked: is [produce] that one gathers for the wine-press made susceptible [to impurity] or not? On this Shammai said: it is made susceptible; and Hillel said: it is not made susceptible. Hillel said to Shammai: Why do they gather grapes in purity, but do not harvest olives in purity? He said to him: If you provoke me, I will decree impurity on the olive harvest too. In this incident we see before our eyes Hillel in his calmness of spirit and Shammai in his strictness: Hillel weighs his opinion on the scales of reason, and Shammai comes with a strong hand and with strictness. And on that day strictness overcame forbearance, for on that day Hillel was bowed before Shammai (Shabbat 17a).{v1_09_19:2} But for the honor of the love of truth of our forebears we will think that it was not because of Shammai's strong hand that Hillel yielded and his opinion was set aside. Rather, without doubt they acted according to the line of the law and according to the halakhah: they stood for a count, and in that assembly those who agreed with Shammai's opinion were the majority; and this is the reason why Hillel bowed his head on that day before Shammai. More than Shammai's strictness, the zeal of Shammai's disciples caused Hillel grief of soul. His great humility and the love of peace that was a crown to his head, these worked against him. For there are people who do not know how to value the worth of such virtues and qualities in others, and they think that a man who deals with them in humility and in love of peace does not do so because he is truly humble and a lover of peace, but because he knows his own shortcomings and knows the weakness of his soul. So it was with the disciples of Shammai: when they saw that Hillel was gentle and meek and set aside his opinion before the opinion of others, they did not ascribe this to his humility and his love of peace, but thought that Hillel's forbearance came from his knowledge of the weakness of his soul and from lack of power to maintain his system against the system of his opponents. For this reason they sometimes banded together against him, and when they saw his wish and effort to appease them, they said in their hearts: We have defeated him! Once Hillel brought his burnt-offering to the Temple court on a festival and laid his hands on it. The disciples of Shammai banded together against him.... and he said to them: It is a female, and I brought it as a peace-offering; and they went away (Betzah 20b;⚠1 Yerushalmi Hagigah 2:3; Tosefta there, ch. 2). Here he changed the truth for the sake of peace, for in truth it was not a female and he did not bring it as a peace-offering. But they, seeing that he appeased them and almost submitted before them, blessed themselves in their hearts, thinking that Hillel recognized that the learning of Shammai was too strong for him, and that he had set aside his opinion before theirs in the dispute over the laying on of hands. They thought that their hand had prevailed over Hillel, until they sought to fix the halakhah according to their words; and their thought had almost gone out into action, had there not been there one of Shammai's disciples who was not hasty of mind like his companions. He recognized that what Hillel did, he did only out of his humility and his love of peace. This man was Bava ben Buti; he knew that the halakhah is according to Hillel, and he was zealous with the zeal of truth and fixed the halakhah according to Hillel.

1.note: Printed 20b (colon); the story of Hillel's burnt-offering begins on Betzah 20a. Kept as printed.

rows.en: Apart from the quality of humility, in which Hillel went to the extreme, his way in his other qualities and deeds was the way of the mean. Therefore he did not love piety that goes beyond the bound of the mean (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 12). Indeed, in all his deeds he took great care not to depart from the custom of the people, and he praises this quality in a fine image, saying: "Do not appear naked and do not appear clothed, do not appear standing and do not appear sitting, do not appear laughing and do not appear weeping, as it is said: a time to laugh" [Ecclesiastes 3:4] (Tosefta Berakhot ch. 2). By this he warns people to conduct themselves at all times according to the custom of the people with whom one sits and in their company (Tractate Derekh Eretz Zuta ch. 5). And it is very likely that what Hillel said elsewhere (Avot ch. 2), "Do not separate yourself from the community," means that one should not deviate from the custom of the people among whom one lives and with whom one conducts oneself. This saying has nothing to do with their saying "one who separates from the ways of the community," which is aimed at one who separates from the ways of the community in matters of faith and religion. Now if we look at all the qualities that were like a crown of glory to his soul, it is no wonder that the heart of all Israel was with him. His grace too stood him in good stead, so that Herod was at peace with him, until not even a slight hint is found that he stirred up strife with him. He too guarded himself from defying this wicked man. Yet one deed that Herod did was without doubt displeasing to Hillel too. From the days when they came up from the exile, they had in their hands a book of genealogies. Herod commanded that this book of lineage be burned.{v1_09_20:1} This matter was evil in Hillel's eyes, for the lineage of Hillel's own family, which was traced back to David king of Israel, was burned with it. (And perhaps at that time Hillel taught (Kiddushin 75a)⚠1 "Ten genealogical classes came up from Babylonia"; and perhaps this mishnah is a copy from the burned book of lineage.) This evil deed was the cause of a new enactment. Formerly in Israel, when the book of lineage was in the Temple, that book gave testimony for every single family, and all inquiry and investigation was superfluous; but from the time Herod destroyed it, inquiry took the place of the testimony from the book. Therefore from that time it also became the rule to seat a court behind the house of the veil, where they examined the lineages of the priesthood.{v1_09_20:2} This court was made up of priests, for they knew who belonged by descent to their tribe, and it was called: the court of priests. And without doubt they judged other matters too, especially those touching the laws of the priests and their rules.

1.note: The mishnah 'Ten genealogical classes came up from Babylonia' (Kiddushin 4:1) stands at Kiddushin 69a; kept as printed.

rows.en: Concerning Hillel's death, one saying has reached us from the eulogy they spoke over him: "Alas, the pious one! Alas, the humble one, disciple of Ezra!" (Sotah 48b; and there in the Yerushalmi, and in the Tosefta ch. 13). These few words tell the whole strength of his deeds and his character. In them his piety and his humility are portrayed: for he was pious in all his deeds, and humble without equal among the sages of his generation; and they compared him to Ezra because he was held to have restored the Torah to its former state, like Ezra in his generation. About sixty years before the destruction of the Temple was the year of his death. Of Shammai's death nothing has been told us. But from two matters that are told it appears that Shammai died before Hillel. The first: from the incident that befell Hillel with the disciples of Shammai, and their fixing the halakhah according to Hillel; in that whole story Shammai is no longer mentioned. The second: from what is told us, that once they wanted to appoint a certain sage as head of the court; and we have no time more fitting than the end of Hillel's days in which that sage could have lived. Therefore the conjecture is close that Shammai died in Hillel's lifetime, and they wanted to appoint another head of the court in his place (*Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 57).

This sage was Akavya ben Mahalalel. He was glorious in honored virtues, and they said of him that the Temple court was not closed upon any man in Israel equal to him in wisdom and in fear of sin. His lifetime falls before the destruction of the Temple, in the generation after the death of Shemaiah and Avtalyon. Of these two sages he spoke harsh words, not as a disciple speaks of his master, which is a sign that he was not among those who came to their house of study. No more than five halakhot of his are known.{v1_09_21:1} And it is no wonder, after they so extolled his wisdom, how it happened that nothing more than these halakhot is left to us; for it is true that the sages of his generation were not pleased with him. They said of him that he was excommunicated by his colleagues because he opened his mouth to speak harsh words against Shemaiah and Avtalyon. And had they not wished to make his affair known to the generations, in order to teach them a moral lesson, these halakhot too would not have reached us. For so it is told: they sent to him, saying: Retract four things [that you say], and we will make you head of the court. He said to them: It is better for me to be called a fool all my days than to be wicked for one hour before the Omnipresent. But the reason why he did not want to retract the four things, he himself has explained to us in his testament to his son. For when his days drew near to die, he said to his son: Retract the four things that I used to say. And when his son asked him: And why did you not retract? he answered him: I heard from the many and they heard from the many; I stood by what I heard and they stood by what they heard. But you have heard from an individual and from the many; it is better to leave the words of the individual and to act according to the words of the many. From this it appears that in Akavya's days there was a dispute of many against many about these halakhot; and if it is true that he lived in the days of Shammai and Hillel, this will be proof that the division among the Pharisees had already begun then. And indeed it also appears from this that at the end of his days they tried to join the division together; for, as emerges from Akavya's words, he alone held to his tradition, and all the sages of the generation disagreed with him. Perhaps this union was the work of Bava ben Buti, who was zealous for Hillel's teaching and succeeded in fixing the halakhah according to him. But the union was not whole and complete, as is seen from the dispute that persisted between the disciples of Shammai and Hillel. Of the events of Akavya's life nothing is known but this little, but it is enough to show us the character of his soul and his qualities. Not many are like him, who would cast authority away and choose to sit low rather than reverse their opinions and thoughts. In agreement with this deed is one of the moral sayings told in his name (Avot 3:1): Consider three things and you will not come into the hands of transgression: know from where you came, and where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give judgment and reckoning. And one who teaches such a lesson, what are authority and honor worth in his eyes? Beyond his quality of humility and fear of God, the quality of love of justice and uprightness adorned him. This we recognize from the answer he gave to his son when he was about to die. At that time his son asked him to commend him to his colleagues, but Akavya did not want this, for he said that it is not of the quality of justice and uprightness that a father should try to incline the hearts of others toward his son by the father's merit; rather it is a man's own merit that will win him grace and favor from others. Therefore he said to his son: Your deeds will bring you near, and your deeds will keep you far.

Here before us is a span of time of about half a century in which the ways of the Oral Torah began to go on new paths. These days are no longer like the first days. The strong bond that held all the Pharisees to be of one heart and one mind slackened little by little. The effort of the leaders to uphold the teaching of the elders against the opposition of the Sadducees did not attain its aim, for the ways they chose for themselves found opponents even among the Pharisees. These ways were two. The first: the widening of the midrash of the Torah in a manner that had no precedent. The second: the clarification of the halakhot of their forebears, to find their reason and their ground. Both these ways found opponents and achieved the very opposite of what they wanted. They wanted to reconcile the opinions, and they caused dispute. The disciples of Shammai and Hillel began to multiply disputes, and these were not passing disputes but lasting ones; for from that time they have not ceased, and God knows how much longer!
The House of Shammai — the House of Hillel —

Shammai and Hillel founded two houses for midrash and for halakhah, and they brought the Oral Torah to a new level. We have already seen that inquiry into the Torah and into the halakhah widened. In the midrash of the Torah they were occupied with finding the source of the halakhah, and they also tried to clarify the halakhot by their dialectic. Hillel investigated and inquired to grasp the reason of each halakhah, and according to his reasoning he judged whether it should stand or be set aside. But to Shammai every ancient halakhah was a statute not to be transgressed, and he tried with his dialectic to give it standing in every matter and in every way. So it emerges from the words told in their names, and it will become still clearer from the disputes of the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai, a great part of which may be ascribed to their time. Before that time there was no dispute in Israel, and the reason has already been made known to us why from their time the bond of agreement was loosened. "The beginning of strife is as when one lets out water" [Proverbs 17:14], and among the disciples it became a flooding river. But the fruit of the dispute was the widening of the halakhot without end. And like the sight we saw in the opposition of the Sadducees, which was a cause for the increase and widening of the halakhot, so that new laws were born, so we will see in the dispute of the Houses: it was the mother of new statutes that the ancients had not imagined. Of Hillel's disciples who sat before him two are mentioned by name: Jonathan ben Uzziel, the greatest among them, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, the least among them. Jonathan ben Uzziel they praised greatly and extolled his learning (Sukkah 28a), but we have from him no halakhic statement that he taught; only from a deed that he did is a halakhic statement learned (Bava Batra 134a). To him they ascribed the Targum of the Prophets (Megillah 3a); but whether the Targum as we have it is from him still needs proof.{v1_09_22:1} R. Yoḥanan, the least: Hillel himself called him father of wisdom and father of generations (Yerushalmi Nedarim 5:7, and Bavli Sukkah there); and it is true that he became a father of generations, and he saved the remnant of Israel from destruction. There was yet another sage who lived at that time and is mentioned by name, and he was a disciple of Hillel: Yoḥanan ben ha-Ḥoroni.{v1_09_22:2} No halakhot are mentioned in his name, but it is told of him that once the elders of the House of Shammai and the elders of the House of Hillel went to visit him and found him sitting with his head and most of his body in the sukkah and his table inside the house; and the elders of the House of Shammai said to him: If you used to act so, you never fulfilled the commandment of the sukkah in your life (Sukkah 2:6).⚠1 The sense of these words shows that Yoḥanan was not of the House of Shammai. And once he did not want to accept moist olives from R. Zadok for fear of impurity, for he thought that R. Zadok followed the House of Shammai, since he was one of them; until he appeased Yoḥanan and said that although he is a disciple of the House of Shammai, all the same he acts only according to the words of the House of Hillel (Yevamot 15b; Tosefta Sukkah ch. 2). We see from this that Yoḥanan ha-Ḥoroni was of the House of Hillel and R. Zadok of the House of Shammai. Of Shammai's disciples four are named. The first is R. Zadok, as we proved above, and he clung with all his strength to the House of Hillel, as will become clear further from his history. The second was Bava ben Buti, a pious man, greatly honored, whose words were heeded among his people. Herod blinded his eyes and killed most of his family (*Antiquities*). And after Herod had taken the light of his eyes, he went himself secretly to his house and disguised himself to him, in order to probe his opinion about him and about his rule; and when he recognized from his words that Bava ben Buti had no intention to do him evil or harm, neither in deed nor in word, Herod turned to him for good, and perhaps in his heart he regretted the evil he had done him; and from that day on he took counsel with Bava from time to time (Bava Batra 4b). He was more God-fearing than many and trembled at the word of the Lord{v1_10_02:1} (Keritot 6:3). And they greatly extolled his piety and his forbearance (Nedarim 66b). Particular halakhot we do not have from him, only one tradition that he handed down in the name of Shammai the Elder (Gittin 57b). Although he was of Shammai's disciples, all the same he followed the House of Hillel, and he was the one who worked to fix the halakhah according to the House of Hillel (Betzah 20b; Yerushalmi Hagigah 2:3; Tosefta there, ch. 2). The third was Dosetai of Kefar Yatmah; he brought one halakhah in the name of Shammai (Orlah 2:5) to refute the words of his colleagues of the House of Shammai and to uphold the words of the House of Hillel. The fourth was Yo'ezer of the Birah. He was one of Shammai's disciples and lived in the days of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, who was head of the House of Hillel; and he brought from him a halakhah which he agreed with and accepted (Orlah 2:12).

1.note: The story of Yoḥanan ha-Ḥoroni in the sukkah is Mishnah Sukkah 2:7; kept as printed.

rows.en: Of the halakhot mentioned in the name of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, some may be ascribed to the time of Shammai and Hillel or close after their death, and most of them were taught during the time from the death of these two leaders until the destruction of the Temple. For when the Temple was destroyed, the name of the House of Shammai sank away entirely, because all the sages joined into one fellowship to strive for freedom of inquiry, even though they did not agree on one opinion in the study of the Torah; and then the houses of study multiplied. The difference of opinions between these two Houses became a stumbling block for the study of the Oral Torah, so that later [sages] complained of the change by which the times had changed: at first there was no dispute in Israel, but when the disciples of Shammai and Hillel who had not served [their masters] sufficiently multiplied, disputes multiplied in Israel and the Torah became like two Torahs (Sanhedrin 88b, and the Yerushalmi and Tosefta there, and in many places). And from then on disputes did not cease, even after the Houses ceased. The aim of both was to uphold religion according to the views of the Pharisees and to make a fence for the Torah, but they differed in the choice of the way to reach that aim. The character of their teachings is easily recognized if we consider the nature of their disputes. The number of their sayings in all is three hundred and sixteen. They are of three kinds: halakhot, midrashim, and fences. The number of halakhot is two hundred and twenty-one; the number of midrashim, twenty-nine; and the number of fences, sixty-six. Their disputes, by the orders of the Mishnah, are as follows. In the order Zera'im there are thirty-five halakhot,{v1_10_03:1} in seven of which the House of Shammai is lenient, and in all the rest the House of Hillel is lenient, except one in which the House of Hillel retracted to teach according to the words of the House of Shammai.{v1_10_03:2} In this order seven disputes in midrash are found, three of them among the leniencies of the House of Shammai,{v1_10_03:3} and sixteen in fences.{v1_10_03:4} So the number of their sayings in the order Zera'im is sixty-six.⚠1 In the order Mo'ed fifty-two of their halakhot are found, and six of them are among the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_03:5} eight disputes in midrash, and among them one of the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_03:6} and there are seventeen fences.{v1_10_03:7} So the sum of their sayings in the order Mo'ed is seventy-seven. In the order Nashim forty-four halakhot of theirs are found, and twelve of them are among the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_03:8} five disputes in midrash, and among them three of the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_03:9} and in fences there are eight, two of them among the leniencies of the House of Shammai.{v1_10_03:10} So the sum of their sayings in the order Nashim is fifty-seven, and in four the House of Hillel retracted to teach according to the House of Shammai. In the order Nezikin there are eleven halakhot, and six of them are among the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_04:1} two in midrash;{v1_10_04:2} and in fences there are six, five of which are among the leniencies of the House of Shammai, and in one the House of Hillel retracted and taught according to the House of Shammai.{v1_10_04:3} In the order Kodashim, seven disputes in halakhah, two of them among the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_04:4} seven in midrash;{v1_10_04:5} and one in fences, among the leniencies of the House of Shammai;{v1_10_04:6} the sum of all of them is fifteen. In the order Tohorot their disputes in halakhah are sixty-five, and among them seven of the leniencies of the House of Shammai, and in one the House of Hillel retracted to teach according to the House of Shammai;{v1_10_04:7} in fences there are eighteen, and in one the House of Hillel retracted to teach according to the House of Shammai.{v1_10_04:8} Now in this great number of halakhot over which the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel disagreed, only fifty-five places are found in which the House of Shammai went to leniency and the House of Hillel to stringency. Most of the places where the House of Hillel is stringent are in halakhah or in midrash, and few of them in fences and decrees. And mostly, in this small number too, the stringency was a necessary consequence of some opinion or midrash that they held elsewhere. For example, if we find that the House of Hillel forbid a man to dismiss [his wife] with an old bill of divorce (Gittin 8:4), and require a second bill of divorce for one who divorced his wife and lodged with her in an inn (there, mishnah 9), this is only a consequence of its midrash, in which it expounded that a man may divorce his wife even if she burned his dish (there 9:10). Therefore by law one must be concerned, if he lodged together with her after a time when his anger had already subsided, that perhaps his desire for her awoke as in the first days and he had relations with her. For this reason too he may not dismiss his wife with an old bill of divorce, that is, when he was alone with her after the bill of divorce was written (see the Yerushalmi and *Tosafot Yom Tov*). So too his other fences rested on reasoning, if we consider them. In most of the disputes that we have recorded among the stringencies of the House of Hillel, this is not the opinion of all the sages; rather other sages disagree and say that the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel did not disagree on this matter, or that they did not accept the dispute.{v1_10_04:9}

1.he: הנה מספר מאמריהם בסדר זרעים ששים וששה
1.note: 35 halakhot + 7 midrashim + 16 fences = 58, not 66; the other orders add up. Kept as printed.

footnotes.en: See Yerushalmi Shevi'it ch. 4 and Sanhedrin ch. 3, and Bavli Sanhedrin (26a), in Tosafot there, s.v. mi-she-rabbu, and in *Tosafot Yom Tov*, Shevi'it 4:2. As for what Tosafot wrote in their first answer, that they permitted it only for the Sabbatical year in our time, which is [only] rabbinic: this reason does not apply to the time of Hillel and Shammai. For in the early days, when the opposition of the Sadducees was still in its strength, they certainly were not lenient in any enactment whose root is from the Torah and which was put in order in the days of the first Scribes. On the contrary, they gave such words of the Scribes more strength than those of the Torah. Therefore also what the authors of the Gemara in Gittin, and the Yerushalmi in the last chapter of Shevi'it, thought, in order to defend Hillel, who enacted the prosbul against the law of the Torah, when they said that the release of debts in Second Temple times was only from the words of the Scribes, is not a defense that holds; for certainly from this side Hillel would not have been lenient in the matter, so as not to give the Sadducees a hold.⚠1 But the authors of the Gemara judged the matter according to their own time. Rava in Gittin already understood that this cannot be Hillel's reason, and said that in truth in money matters the sages have the power to act as they see fit, even against the law of the Torah; and so Rashi explains there.

1.note: Literally 'so as not to give the Sadducees [occasion] to rule/subdue'; rendered 'a hold'.

footnotes.en: In the Bavli, Shabbat, they added: they stuck a sword in the house of study and said, Whoever would come in, let him come in, and whoever would go out, let him not go out; and that day was as hard for Israel as the day on which the calf was made. But from the Yerushalmi and the Tosefta it appears that this took place at the decree of the eighteen things.
Jost, *Geschichte des Judenthums und seiner Secten*, 323, note 1, on the basis of the words of Sachs, *Beiträge*, part 2, 156.

In Middot 5:4 we learned: the Chamber of Hewn Stone, there the Sanhedrin sat and judged the priesthood. And in Kiddushin (76b) they said: there sat those who traced the lineage of priesthood and Levites; and Rashi explained: in the Chamber of Hewn Stone etc., and he means the mishnah of Middot. This needs study, for they did not say there explicitly "the Sanhedrin sat," as in the reading of the mishnah. Moreover, the phrase "those who traced the lineage of priesthood" shows that it speaks of a special office, and it appears from this that for the purpose of examining the lineages of the priesthood there was a special court. And indeed this is stated in Sifrei, Korah, piska 116: "And you and your sons with you shall keep your priesthood for everything of the altar and within the veil" [Numbers 18:7]: from here they said, there was a place behind the house of the veil where they examined the lineages of the priesthood. So those who traced the lineage of the priesthood sat in a special place, and that is behind the house of the veil. And who were those who kept the priesthood, that is, the lineages of the priesthood? Aaron and his sons. And although in the Tosefta too, Hagigah ch. 2, the reading is "in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the lineages of priesthood and the lineages of Levites sit," it appears that this too is not exact, and the main thing is as stated in the Sifrei; and in the Sifrei the intent was necessarily not the Chamber of Hewn Stone, for if so it would not say "there was a place." Now this is the source for our conjecture that there was a special place behind the house of the veil where those who traced the lineage of the priesthood sat, and these tracers who examined were priests; and this is the court of priests mentioned in Ketubot 1:5⚠1 and Rosh Hashanah 1:6.⚠2 And see what I wrote on this point in a special article in the Hebrew periodical *Ha-Maggid* of the year 5627.

1.note: The mishnah number is blurred in the scan; read as 1:5, where the court of priests is named.

2.note: The court of priests is in Rosh Hashanah 1:7; kept as printed.

footnotes.en: All these events come from two mishnayot in Eduyyot 5:6 and 5:7, see there. And there four halakhot of his are taught; and see also Niddah 2:6, Nega'im 5:3, Bekhorot 3:4, Berakhot (19a). The fifth is in Nega'im 1:4, and on that one they did not ask him to retract, because he neither forbade nor permitted anything; and see *Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 56.
See Zunz in the book *G[ottesdienstliche] V[orträge]* p. 63, and R. Abraham Geiger in the book *U[rschrift]* p. 164; and see below, ch. 22.

R. Z. Frankel, in *Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 53 note 8, counts Yoḥanan ha-Ḥoroni among the disciples of Shammai and does not count R. Zadok at all. But this is not so. For these are the words of the Gemara: "R. Eleazar ben Zadok says: When I was studying Torah with Yoḥanan ha-Ḥoroni, I saw that he ate dry bread with salt in years of drought. I came and told Father. He said to me: Take him olives. I took them to him; he saw that they were moist. He said to me: I do not eat [moist] olives [so the reading of the Tosefta]. I came and told Father. He said to me: Go, tell him: the jar was pierced, only the lees had stopped it up. And although he was a disciple of Shammai, he acted only according to the words of the House of Hillel." R. Z. Frankel thought that the statement "although he was a disciple of Shammai" refers to Yoḥanan, and this against the opinion of Tosafot s.v. amar. But in the Tosefta it is proved explicitly that this statement refers to R. Zadok, for there the reading is: "R. Eleazar ben Zadok said etc. He (his father) said to me: Go, tell him, it was pierced according to the words of the House of Hillel, only the lees had stopped it up; to inform you that he ate ordinary food in purity; for although he was among the disciples of Shammai, he behaved only according to the House of Hillel." And so it is in Tosefta Eduyyot ch. 2. From this wording it is proved clearly that "to inform you" refers to R. Zadok, and this is the meaning: Yoḥanan ha-Ḥoroni, when he saw the olives moist, feared that they had become impure, for he thought that R. Zadok surely behaved like his teachers, the House of Shammai; but he (Yoḥanan), who was of the House of Hillel, feared this. [R. Zadok] sent him word not to fear, since it was pierced according to the words of the House of Hillel. On this they added in the baraita that there is no wonder at what R. Zadok did according to the House of Hillel, for although he (R. Zadok) was a disciple of Shammai, he acted only according to the words of the House of Hillel. This is the meaning of the Tosefta without any doubt, and this is also the meaning of the words of the Gemara, and so Tosafot understood it there.

There we learned: Bava ben Buta used to offer a voluntary suspensive guilt-offering every day, except the day after Yom Kippur. One day he said: By this Temple! If they let me, I would bring one; but they say to me: Wait until you come into a case of doubt. Here we have before us an event that took place: Bava ben Buti offered a voluntary suspensive guilt-offering every day, and the priests in the Temple offered it, except on the day after Yom Kippur, when they told him to wait. On this R. Eliezer relied, and established the halakhah that a man may offer a suspensive guilt-offering voluntarily every day. But the Sages disagree and say that a suspensive guilt-offering is brought only for a matter whose deliberate transgression incurs karet. How then will they account for that event? Surely they did not deny R. Eliezer, and admitted that the event happened so; and if it was so, are not their words contradicted? Necessarily, even if by the strict line of the law it is as the Sages said, in practice they did not act so while the Temple stood.
